# Reconstructing the Internet Research Agency’s 2016 Social-Media Influence Operation

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports the conclusion that the Internet Research Agency (IRA) conducted a centrally funded, multi-platform influence operation directed at U.S. political and social audiences. The operation was not limited to publishing pro-Donald Trump material or purchasing online advertisements. Its broader objective, as reconstructed from the Department of Justice (DOJ) indictment and Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI) findings, was to exploit existing American political, racial, religious, and cultural divisions; damage Hillary Clinton’s candidacy; support Donald Trump before the election; discourage some minority and likely Democratic voters from participating; and undermine confidence in U.S. democratic institutions.

The DOJ indictment describes an alleged criminal conspiracy involving the IRA, entities associated with Yevgeniy Prigozhin, and multiple named employees. The SSCI report, based partly on data supplied by social-media companies, independently assessed that the Russian government tasked and supported the IRA’s interference efforts. The evidence indicates a professionalized operation that combined human operators, false American personas, platform-specific tactics, paid advertising, organic posts, direct communication with Americans, and the organization of real-world political events. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Source basis and evidentiary status

The evidence should be separated into three categories:

| Evidence category | Main source | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| Criminal allegations | DOJ indictment, February 2018 | Detailed allegations concerning organizational structure, personnel, funding, accounts, personas, activities, and alleged offenses |
| Congressional findings and assessments | SSCI Volume 2 | Findings based on oversight, platform data, law-enforcement information, intelligence reporting, and expert analysis |
| Platform-data analysis | Howard et al. report | Quantitative analysis of IRA activity on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube using data supplied to the SSCI |

The DOJ indictment contains allegations rather than adjudicated findings. The named defendants were charged, and the indictment itself should not be treated as proof of every allegation. By contrast, the SSCI report presents committee findings and assessments, while also acknowledging that the committee relied substantially on social-media companies’ attribution of accounts and that the full scope of IRA activity remains unknown. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Organizational structure and funding

The DOJ alleged that the IRA was a Russian organization headquartered in St. Petersburg and operating from 55 Savushkina Street. It allegedly employed hundreds of people and maintained specialized departments for graphics, data analysis, search-engine optimization, information technology, and finance. A U.S.-focused “translator project” was reportedly created in or around April 2014 and had more than 80 employees by July 2016. The indictment also alleges that the organization’s stated objective included conducting “information warfare against the United States of America” and spreading distrust toward candidates and the political system. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The alleged funding structure connected the IRA to Yevgeniy Prigozhin and companies he controlled, including Concord Management and Consulting and Concord Catering. The indictment characterizes Concord as the IRA’s primary funding source and describes the wider effort as “Project Lakhta.” By September 2016, the monthly Project Lakhta budget allegedly exceeded 73 million Russian rubles, described in the indictment as more than $1.25 million at the time. The indictment further alleges that funds were routed through approximately fourteen affiliate bank accounts and disguised as payments for software support and development. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The SSCI report reached a broader assessment that the IRA was funded and directed by Prigozhin and that the operation was conducted at the direction of the Kremlin. The committee based this assessment on the alleged relationship between Prigozhin and the IRA, the scope and objectives of the campaign, and the relationship between the IRA’s conduct and other Russian government interference activities. This is a congressional assessment, not a judicial finding in the provided materials. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Intelligence gathering and preparation

The operation appears to have begun as a sustained research and preparation effort rather than a short-term election advertising campaign. The DOJ alleged that IRA personnel monitored U.S. social-media groups, measured audience size and engagement, and studied U.S. political and social issues. The indictment also alleges that Aleksandra Krylova and Anna Bogacheva traveled through several U.S. states in June 2014 under false pretenses to collect intelligence, using equipment including cameras, SIM cards, and “drop phones.” ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The SSCI report similarly describes the 2014 trip as an intelligence-gathering mission intended to inform later influence operations. According to the committee, the trip formed part of a wider effort to understand American political divisions, identify useful audiences, impersonate U.S. citizens, and improve the operation’s tactics. The evidence therefore supports a planning model in which online activity was preceded by audience research and operational preparation. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

The indictment further alleges that IRA employees used U.S.-based servers and virtual private networks to conceal Russian origins, registered email accounts under false names, and operated on U.S. platforms while presenting themselves as Americans. These methods were intended to create the appearance of domestic grassroots activity and reduce the likelihood that platforms, regulators, journalists, or users would identify the operation as foreign-controlled. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

## Personas, pages, and audience cultivation

A central feature of the operation was the construction of apparently authentic American identities. IRA specialists allegedly created social-media accounts that appeared to belong to U.S. individuals, local activists, political organizations, or community groups. Operators were divided into day and night shifts and were instructed to post according to U.S. time zones and holidays. The alleged purpose was to make the accounts appear to be operated by Americans rather than by Russian personnel working from St. Petersburg. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The operation used both right-leaning and left-leaning identities. Named or identified properties included “Blacktivist,” “Being Patriotic,” “Heart of Texas,” “United Muslims of America,” “Army of Jesus,” “South United,” “Secured Borders,” and the Twitter account @TEN_GOP. The apparent ideological diversity was not evidence of independent grassroots organization. The Senate report assessed that IRA operators used personas on opposing sides of debates in order to intensify conflict and divide audiences. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

This strategy involved audience cultivation before the delivery of more explicitly political material. The SSCI report described a pattern in which accounts first posted ordinary or identity-confirming content to establish credibility, then introduced more divisive “payload” messages at strategically selected moments. The “Army of Jesus” example illustrates this approach: religious and devotional material was interspersed with a claim attacking Hillary Clinton. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Political objectives and narratives

The evidence supports four principal objectives.

### 1. Supporting Trump and damaging Clinton

The DOJ alleged that by early or mid-2016 the IRA’s operations supported Trump and disparaged Clinton. It cited internal instructions to criticize Clinton and other candidates while exempting Bernie Sanders and Trump. The indictment also lists pro-Trump and anti-Clinton hashtags and advertisements. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The SSCI found that IRA activity was “overtly and almost invariably supportive” of Trump and harmful to Clinton. It also found that Clinton was uniquely and consistently targeted negatively, including by personas that otherwise represented different ideological positions. The committee’s finding is consistent with the conclusion that the operation used both direct candidate advocacy and indirect attacks on Clinton’s credibility and electability. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

### 2. Suppressing or diverting votes

The indictment describes messages directed at minority audiences encouraging nonparticipation or support for third-party candidate Jill Stein. Examples include “vote for Jill Stein” messages and statements urging Black voters not to vote. The SSCI report assessed that voter-suppression narratives targeted nonwhite and likely Clinton voters, while right-leaning audiences were more often encouraged to support Trump. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

### 3. Exploiting race and social divisions

Race was the most prominent operational theme identified by the SSCI. More than 66 percent of the Facebook advertisements in the committee’s analysis reportedly contained a race-related term. “Blacktivist” generated approximately 11.2 million Facebook engagements, and five of the ten leading IRA Instagram accounts focused on African-American issues or audiences. The report also states that 96 percent of IRA YouTube content concerned race or police brutality. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

The operation also addressed immigration, religion, police conduct, gender identity, the Second Amendment, Southern identity, and veterans. The point was not necessarily to persuade every audience toward a consistent Russian ideological position. Rather, the evidence indicates an effort to identify existing fault lines and make them more emotionally and politically consequential. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S4](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/senatedocs/1/))

### 4. Undermining trust

The operation’s broader goal was to produce distrust in candidates, political parties, government institutions, and the electoral process. The DOJ alleged that the IRA sought to “sow discord” in the U.S. political system. The SSCI described the campaign as extending beyond the election itself and seeking to weaken Americans’ relationships with one another and with democratic institutions. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))
